title: Read to the sick
hookLine: ten perceptions read to the sick monk Girimananda, who recovers

lines: WHAT DO WE BRING THE SICK?
ANANDA IS SENT WITH A LIST.
cards: When someone we love is sick, we bring things: soup, flowers, a phone charger, a magazine nobody reads. What we really want to bring is something that helps, and we often don't know what that is.
In the Book of Tens, a monk named Girimananda is sick, in pain, gravely ill. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, asks the Buddha to visit him, out of compassion. The Buddha does something unexpected.
He doesn't go himself. He sends Ananda back with something to bring: not medicine, but a list of ten things to read aloud.

teach.b: If you tell Girimananda the ten perceptions, the Buddha says, it's possible his illness will subside at once. Then he gives them.

One, impermanence: the body, feelings, all of it, changing. Two, not-self: none of it is me or mine. Three, the unattractive: the body seen plainly, hair, skin, bones, the inside as well as the outside.
Four, drawbacks: the body as a home for many illnesses, and the text names a long list of them, eye disease to fever. Five, abandoning: letting go of harmful thoughts. Six, dispassion.
Seven, cessation. Eight, not delighting in the whole world. Nine, the impermanence of all that's made.
Ten, mindfulness of breathing, given in full: breathing in long, breathing out long, and on through sixteen steps.
Ananda learns them, goes to Girimananda and recites them, and the text says Girimananda recovered from that illness. It isn't comforting in the usual way. It doesn't say you'll be fine.
It looks straight at the body, its fragility and its changes, and ends with the simplest thing a sick person can still do: breathe, and know they're breathing.
One modern reading is that a mind steadied and less gripped by fear helps the body.
The text itself doesn't explain it; it just says he recovered. In some Theravada communities, this sutta is still chanted for people who are ill.

how: In parts of the Theravada world, monks chant the Girimananda Sutta for the sick, and visiting and reading to ill people, lay or ordained, is a long-standing Buddhist act of care.

games.q: you're the Buddha. Ananda asks you to visit a gravely sick monk. what do you do?
o: send Ananda with ten perceptions to recite.
tell Ananda the monk must bear it.
games.why: he teaches Ananda the ten perceptions to carry to the bedside. Ananda recites them, and Girimananda recovers.

practice: Settle with the tenth perception: breathing in long, know it; breathing out long, know it.
Then bring to mind someone who is unwell, near or far, and picture sitting beside them, wondering what line, message or memory might steady them. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.

wordCard.voice: sanna. The Pali word for perception, as in the ten perceptions Ananda carries to Girimananda's bedside in the Book of Tens, from impermanence to mindfulness of breathing, after which the monk recovers. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sanna: perception, recognition; the ten sanna are the ten perceptions.

carryVoice: Your line: ten perceptions. Ten things to read aloud, and the last one is simply a breath. Day six hundred seventy-three.
